questions.question: What does a Chaum–Pedersen (DLEQ) proof aim to show?
options: That log_g(y1) equals log_h(y2) without revealing the shared exponent
That y1 and y2 are uniformly random elements of the group
That the prover can compute discrete logs for arbitrary group elements
That the verifier learns the secret exponent x as part of verification
questions.explanation: A DLEQ proof shows both public values use the same secret exponent x, while keeping x hidden.

questions.question: In the Chaum–Pedersen protocol, what are the prover’s commitments a1 and a2?
options: a1 = g^r and a2 = h^r for a fresh random nonce r
a1 = y1^r and a2 = y2^r for a fresh random nonce r
a1 = g^x and a2 = h^x where x is the witness being proved
a1 = g^c and a2 = h^c where c is the verifier’s challenge
questions.explanation: The prover commits with the same nonce r under both bases: a1=g^r and a2=h^r.

questions.question: Which verification checks define Chaum–Pedersen for y1=g^x and y2=h^x?
options: Check g^s == a1·y1^c and h^s == a2·y2^c (mod p)
Check g^c == a1·y1^s and h^c == a2·y2^s (mod p)
Check g^s == y1·a1^c and h^s == y2·a2^c (mod p)
Check g^x == a1·y1^c and h^x == a2·y2^c (mod p)
questions.explanation: Verification checks the response s is consistent with both commitments and both statement elements under the same challenge c.

questions.question: How does the special HVZK simulator produce an accepting transcript without knowing x?
options: Choose (c, s) first and compute a1, a2 so the verification equations hold
Choose x first and then set y1 and y2 to match the commitments exactly
Choose (a1, a2) first and then solve for a challenge c that makes them verify
Choose a challenge c first and then ask the verifier to reveal the nonce r
questions.explanation: The simulator picks c and s, then back-computes commitments so the verifier’s checks pass without any witness.

questions.question: Two accepting transcripts reuse the same commitments (a1, a2) but have c1 != c2 and responses s1, s2. What is x (mod q)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the two response equations to eliminate the nonce and solve for x using a modular inverse.

questions.question: What catastrophic failure occurs if the prover ever reuses the same nonce r in Chaum–Pedersen?
options: Anyone can extract the witness x from two proofs with different challenges
The verifier can no longer compute the challenge c correctly
The protocol becomes perfectly binding but no longer zero-knowledge
The prover becomes unable to compute commitments a1 and a2 consistently
questions.explanation: Nonce reuse repeats the commitments, and special soundness lets an attacker recover x from two accepting transcripts.

questions.question: For Fiat–Shamir Chaum–Pedersen, what must the hash-based challenge c bind to?
options: A domain tag plus all statement and commitment elements in the transcript
Only the commitments (a1, a2), so the statement can be swapped later
Only the statement (y1, y2), so commitments can be recomputed freely
Only the group parameters (p, q, g, h), since they define the protocol
questions.explanation: The challenge must bind the exact context, statement, and commitments; otherwise proofs can be replayed or transplanted.

questions.question: Why is domain separation (a protocol/version tag) important in Fiat–Shamir transcripts?
options: It prevents the same proof bytes from being valid in a different protocol context
It makes the hash output larger so challenges are automatically stronger
It ensures the prover’s nonce r is uniform even if the RNG is biased
It allows the verifier to skip subgroup checks for performance reasons
questions.explanation: A domain tag makes the challenge protocol-specific, reducing cross-protocol replay and transcript-confusion risks.
